en: The Scripture on Gathering Flowers in Contravention of the King’s Command and Receiving the Prediction from the Buddha, titled *Miaohua* (Wondrous Flower), translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Tanwulan of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
In the past, when the World-Honored One was traveling through Rājagṛha, he preached a sutra that dispels ignorance; its initial words were excellent, as were its middle [words].
The discourse was excellent in its beginning and excellent in its conclusion; its meaning was subtle and profound, it purified the holy life, and what was taught was vast and universal.
At that time, the king provided more than several dozen attendants to constantly gather fine flowers to supply the royal household.

One day, the noble ladies, court maids, and attendants of all ranks within the inner palace went together outside the city to gather flowers. As they were returning toward the city, they encountered the Buddha on the road. From afar, they beheld the World-Honored One, his physical marks and sublime radiance majestic and immeasurable, like the moon among the stars;
he was like the newly risen sun illuminating the world, surrounded by his holy assembly of disciples and bodhisattvas before and behind him.
He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself in salutation, and thought to himself:
"Human life is difficult to preserve; the appearance of a Buddha in the world is difficult to encounter; and the encounter with the sutras and the Dharma is difficult to find."

Now that I have encountered the Great Sage, I am like a sick man who has found a skilled physician; yet my body is already poor and lowly, further burdened by the duties of the state. The hardships of corvée labor never cease, and the king’s demands are strict and urgent. As one assigned to gather flowers, I must always present them early; were I to miss the proper time, I might well be executed.
The sun does not rise twice; the assembly of sages is difficult to encounter, appearing only once in hundreds of millions of ages.

It would be better to sacrifice one’s body and life to offer flowers to the Buddha and scatter them over the assembly of sages, thereby receiving the sutras and precepts, and listening to and contemplating the profound Dharma and infinite wisdom.

Throughout incalculable kalpas, I have been harmed by others beyond measure; yet never for the sake of the Dharma have I begrudged my own body or life. Now, through this karma of making offerings to the World-Honored One and the Triple Gem, even if I am harmed, I shall not fall into suffering but will surely be reborn in a state of peace.
He then scattered flowers over the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones, and having withdrawn, he took refuge with single-minded devotion and prostrated repeatedly.

The Buddha, knowing that his thoughts had given rise to the aspiration for the Great Way (bodhicitta), felt profound compassion for him and fully expounded for him the Mahāyāna Dharma, the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), the four immeasurables, the four debts of gratitude, and the three liberations of the bodhisattva.

At that time, all those who had been gathering flowers conceived the aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; their minds understood the Buddha’s wisdom, reaching the stage of non-retrogression and the state of non-arising.
The Buddha then bestowed upon them the prediction:

"In the future, you shall attain Buddhahood, with the title of Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat. You shall be named Wondrous Flower (Miaohua) Tathāgata."
When those people nearby heard this, there was none who did not rejoice; they received the Great Dharma and made offerings to the Triple Gem.

At that time, the flower-gatherer, having made his offering and received the prediction of enlightenment, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and returned home. He took leave of his parents and wife and children, saying:
"My life has now come to its end; I have been executed by the king."
The parents asked in astonishment,
"What is the offense? The sons replied:

"Sent by the king to gather various flowers, I saw the Buddha from afar and offered him some blossoms. The king was extremely urgent; not only have I failed to meet the appointed time, but I now have no more flowers. My life will surely be in peril."
"Therefore, it was merely a parting of words.
When his parents heard this, they became even more sorrowful and distressed, wondering what could be done.
They opened the chest and looked inside; it was filled with beautiful flowers and various *sumana* scents. The fragrance wafted richly and reached far in all four directions, and the parents said:
"We can present him to the King.
Each of the sons said, "If the common people see him, they will surely pass the word to the King; furthermore, it would be out of season, and we fear we shall not find safety."

At that time, the king became greatly incensed; seeing that [the messenger] had not arrived at the appointed hour and that the many flowers had been scattered, he dispatched a border minister with a large force of soldiers to arrest him and bring him back.
Having received the king’s command, the minister bound the man hand and foot and brought him into the palace, where his crime merited execution by public stoning.
The people were not afraid, and their facial expressions remained unchanged.
The king, finding this strange, questioned them:
"Your transgressions are such that your lives are in jeopardy; you have been bound and brought here to be executed."
"Why are you not afraid, and why has your facial expression not changed?
He then addressed the King, saying:

"In human life there is death, and for all things that come into being there is decay. Throughout countless kalpas, I have constantly acted contrary to the Dharma and have not spared my own body or life. This morning, while gathering flowers, I encountered the World-Honored One; I offered these flowers to him and prostrated myself in refuge."
At that time, knowing that he was to die for violating the command, he thought: "It would be better to die possessing virtue than to live without virtue.
He looked back at the flower basket and saw it was still full as before; this was entirely due to the compassionate grace of the Tathāgata covering him.
The king found this most strange; his mind could not believe it to be true, so he went to the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and with palms joined, asked the Buddha:
"Do you have such an intention?"
The Buddha said, “Indeed, O King!

This man, with a sincere heart, desires to deliver all beings throughout the ten directions and does not begrudge his own body or life; therefore, he has taken these various flowers to scatter over the Buddha. His mind harbors no thought of seeking reward, yet he shall receive the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa). In the future, he shall become a Buddha named Wondrous Flower Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Because he has resolved his great intention and received this prediction, the fragrance of his compassionate heart and his flowers shall fill every basket and vessel, such that there is none who does not hear and know it.”
The king was greatly rejoiced; he quickly untied his many bonds and repented, reproaching himself:
"My foolish mind failed me, and I bound the Bodhisattva; I pray only that you pardon my transgression."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"One who is able to reform themselves is the same as one who has no faults.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the king, his ministers, and the common people were all filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.
This concludes the *Sūtra on Picking Flowers in Disobedience to the King, Offering Them to the Buddha, and Receiving the Prediction of Enlightenment*, titled "Wondrous Flower."
